title: Chapter 20 — The Trade Of Place-Hunting In Certain Democratic Countries
paragraphs: In the United States, as soon as a man has gained some education and some money, he either tries to get rich through commerce or industry, or he buys land in the backwoods and becomes a pioneer. All he asks of the state is that it not disturb his labor and that it keep his earnings safe. Among most European nations, when a man begins to feel his strength and his desires widen, the first thing he thinks of is getting a public job. These opposite effects, which spring from the same cause, deserve a brief look.

When public employments are few, poorly paid, and insecure, while the various lines of business are numerous and profitable, the new and eager desires that the principle of equality produces turn from every side toward business, not toward official duties. But if, while the ranks of society are growing more equal, the education of the people stays incomplete, or their spirit is anything but bold, and if commerce and industry, held back in their growth, offer only slow and difficult ways of making a fortune, then the members of the community, despairing of improving their own condition, rush to the head of the state and demand its help. To relieve their own needs at the expense of the public treasury seems to them the easiest and most open way, if not the only one, to rise above a condition that no longer satisfies them. Place-hunting becomes the most widely followed of all trades. This must be especially so in those great centralized monarchies where paid offices are immensely numerous and the tenure of them fairly secure, so that no one despairs of getting a place and enjoying it as undisturbedly as an inherited fortune.

I will not point out that the universal and excessive desire for office is a great social evil, that it destroys the citizen’s spirit of independence and spreads a venal and servile temper through the whole body of society, and that it stifles the manlier virtues. Nor will I take the trouble to show that this kind of traffic creates only unproductive activity, which stirs up the country without adding to its resources. All of this is obvious. But I would point out that a government that encourages this tendency endangers its own tranquillity and puts its very existence at great risk. I know that in a time like ours, when the love and respect that once attached to authority are seen slowly to fade, it may seem necessary to those in power to hold every man more tightly through his own interest. It may seem convenient to use his own passions to keep him orderly and quiet. But this cannot last. What may look like a source of strength for a time will surely become, in the end, a great cause of embarrassment and weakness.

Among democratic nations, as elsewhere, the number of official appointments has limits in the end, but among those nations the number of aspirants has none. It rises continually, gradually and irresistibly, as social conditions become more equal, and it is checked only by the size of the population. So when public employments offer the only outlet for ambition, the government eventually meets with permanent opposition, because it is charged with satisfying unlimited desires with limited means. It is quite certain that, of all the peoples in the world, the hardest to restrain and to manage is a people of petitioners. Whatever rulers may do, such a people can never be satisfied, and there is always reason to fear that in the end they will overturn the constitution of the country and change the face of the state, for the sole purpose of clearing out places. The sovereigns of the present age try to take upon themselves alone all the new desires that equality arouses, and to satisfy them. Unless I am mistaken, they will come to regret ever embarking on this policy. One day they will find that they have put their own power at risk by making it so necessary, and that the safer and more honest course would have been to teach their subjects the art of providing for themselves. *a

[Footnote a: In fact, more recent experience has shown that place-hunting is just as intense in the United States as in any country in Europe. The Americans themselves regard it as one of the great evils of their social condition, and it strongly affects their political institutions. But the American who seeks a place seeks not so much a means of livelihood as the distinction that office and public employment confer. Where there is no true aristocracy, the public service creates a false one, which is as much an object of ambition as the distinctions of rank in aristocratic countries. — Translator’s Note.]
